name: Carbon180 (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: a tonne of CO₂ removed or kept out of the air spares people everywhere (heat deaths), so the result is spread by world population.
summary: Carbon180, a US non-profit, does policy advocacy, analysis and community regranting for carbon removal; this model counts the federal programmes it worked on that were won or defended in 2020-2025 (the first megaton direct air capture plants under the 2021 Regional DAC Hubs and the 2022 45Q credit, the speed-up those programmes and the Department of Energy's carbon-removal research give the technology worldwide, the larger 45Q credit's capture at other plants, the 2022 law's farm conservation money and the 2021 law's reforestation money) against its spending over those years ($10.06M in 2025). At the defaults a dollar given removes or stores about 0.001 tonnes of CO₂ (about $1,000 a tonne), but the public money behind those tonnes (the $85 and $180 credits, the hub grants, the farm and forest money, the removals bought later) costs its taxpayers more than the tonnes are worth on the site's scale: a net harm of about −0.003 years of healthy life per $1,000. Direct air capture is still small and costly, each win is shared with many groups, companies and what Congress would have done anyway (Carbon180 is credited with 0.3% to 10% of the advocacy behind each), the hubs have been cut back, and the next dollar mostly defends these wins (27% of the period's average). The biggest uncertainties are the shared discount rate and years a won reform counts, how far direct air capture will scale, the public money per tonne and Carbon180's share of each win; every branch is discounted for missing data, since no tonne is measured for its work.

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: What Carbon180 spent: 2025 from its Form 990, and the average year of 2020-2025, the period whose wins are counted.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: Tonnes a year each win would remove or store once in effect: the plants' design capacities, the IEA's pathway and the shared figure for the 45Q credit.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: How much of each win is advocacy's doing, the years it counts and the wait before its tonnes come.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: For each win: what would have happened anyway, Carbon180's share of the advocacy, and how much of the win is delivered; then the evidence and missing-data steps and the side effects.

sections.title: Air pollution these tonnes carry
sections.explainer: Every tonne avoids its heat deaths; a tonne from burning less fossil fuel near people also avoids air-pollution deaths. Removed and stored CO₂ carries none (docs/normalization.md 2.5).

sections.title: Other outcomes, in tonnes
sections.explainer: The public money's cost to its payers (units of value) is counted in its own unit and enters the tonnes only through the site's fixed bridge (docs/normalization.md 2.6).

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: Tonnes of CO₂ removed or stored per year of the period, per dollar of a typical year's cost.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind; and the next dollar does less than the period's average.

Spending grew from $2.7M to $12.0M over the period, so a typical year is well below 2025's.

rows.label: Share of the CO₂ captured that is a net removal, after the energy and materials the plants use
rows.explainer: Life-cycle studies of running plants find 85% (Hinwil, grid power) and 93% (Hellisheiði, geothermal) of the CO₂ captured is a net removal (Deutz & Bardow 2021, Nature Energy 6: 203-213, https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/10.1038/s41560-020-00771-9/abstract: 'carbon capture efficiencies of 85.4% and 93.1%'). The Texas plants burn natural gas for heat and capture its CO₂ too, and its methane leaks count against them, so the low end is lower. Our judgment, 85% (60% to 93%).

Direct air capture worldwide in 2050 on the IEA's net-zero pathway

source.title: IEA (2023), Unlocking the potential of direct air capture: Is scaling up through carbon markets possible?

rows.explainer: Technology line: the yardstick for how far direct air capture could scale (the IEA's 2023 update of its Net Zero Emissions scenario; the 2022 edition had about 980 Mt). A pathway, not a forecast: how much is built and how much the US programmes speed it are rows below.

rows.label: Inflation Reduction Act's larger 45Q credit (2022): CO₂ stored a year at other plants (besides the direct air capture plants above)
rows.explainer: The shared figure for tonnes stored because of the larger credit (facts: climate.ira_45q_capture_tco2_per_year, 60 million tonnes a year, 20 to 185 million), less the direct air capture plants counted in their own branch, so no tonne is counted twice: capture at power plants, ethanol, gas processing and other factories.

source.title: IEA (2023), Unlocking the potential of direct air capture: Is scaling up through carbon markets possible?

rows.explainer: The same pathway's 2030 point, so the level in the years counted can be read off the pathway.

rows.label: Year of the pathway's first point

source.title: IEA (2023), Unlocking the potential of direct air capture: Is scaling up through carbon markets possible?

rows.explainer: The calendar year of the 70 million tonnes.

rows.label: Year of the pathway's second point

source.title: IEA (2023), Unlocking the potential of direct air capture: Is scaling up through carbon markets possible?

rows.explainer: The calendar year of the 600 million tonnes.

rows.label: Technology: public money per tonne for the removals the faster build brings (US$)
rows.explainer: Removals built on the pathway are bought by someone, mostly governments: the US credit pays $180 a tonne (facts: climate.q45_credit_usd_per_tco2_dac), and Europe, Canada and Japan buy removals for their own targets; voluntary buyers (Frontier, Microsoft) pay the rest. Anchor: costs of $100-300 a tonne by the 2040s in the learning studies the IEA cites, against several hundred today. Our judgment, $150 a tonne of public money (60 to 300).

rows.label: Technology: DOE carbon-removal research money a year (US$)
rows.explainer: The Energy Act of 2020's carbon-removal research programmes at the Department of Energy: public money that funds the technology work counted in this branch. Anchor: about $116.5 million a year, held in the 2026 appropriations (Carbon180's own account of the line, row tech_policy_share); our judgment, $116.5 million ($90 to $140 million), since the line is not reported separately in one place.

rows.label: Farm conservation money: acres under climate-focused contracts the Inflation Reduction Act funded in a year (FY2024)

source.title: US Department of Agriculture, farmers.gov (10 January 2025), Shaping a Sustainable Future in 2024
source.quote: These investments cover over 11 million acres in fiscal year 2024

rows.explainer: Land line of the policy work: the law's $19.5 billion for USDA's conservation programmes (EQIP, CSP, RCPP, ACEP) paid more than 23,000 climate-focused contracts in fiscal 2024. USDA doesn't say whether these are new or all acres under contract; the model takes the fiscal-2024 figure as a typical year of acres under contracts in force, with overlapping multi-year contracts and the 2025 rescission netted in the implementation row below.

rows.label: Farm conservation money: CO₂e a funded acre cuts, relative to cover crops' soil carbon
rows.explainer: The contracts mix cover crops with nutrient management, reduced tillage, grazing and forestry practices, several with smaller or less certain effects per acre (no-till's soil-carbon gain is often only a shift to the surface), and a few with more (tree planting). Our judgment, 0.6 (0.3 to 1.2).

rows.label: Farm conservation money: tonnes of CO₂e a year on the funded acres
rows.explainer: Acres in hectares (facts: climate.ha_per_acre) × the shared soil-carbon figure for cover crops (facts: climate.cover_crop_soc_tco2_per_ha_year, 0.7 t CO₂ a hectare a year, 0.1 to 1.5: Poeplau & Don's meta-analysis and a re-analysis of sound trials) × the practice mix: about 1.9 million tonnes a year.

rows.label: Forests: national-forest acres reforested a year since the 2021 law lifted the Reforestation Trust Fund's cap

source.title: Time (17 September 2024), National Forests Are Being Replanted Post-Wildfire Thanks to the Infrastructure Bill
source.quote: In the Act's first two years, the U.S. Forest Service reforested 360,000 acres, reducing the agency's backlog by 10%.

rows.explainer: Forestry part of the policy line: the 2021 infrastructure law's REPLANT provisions lifted the $30 million cap on the Reforestation Trust Fund (about a fivefold increase in yearly funding) and set the Forest Service to clear its 3.6-million-acre backlog within a decade; Carbon180's 2021 report lists these reforestation investments among the provisions 'our policy team helped structure'. 360,000 acres in two years: 180,000 a year. The count includes assisted natural regeneration as well as planting; land that would have regrown anyway is in the counterfactual row, slower regrowth in the evidence row.

rows.label: Forests: CO₂ a replanted hectare takes up a year over its growth
rows.explainer: Cook-Patton et al. (2020, Nature, doi 10.1038/s41586-020-2686-x) map natural forest regrowth rates worldwide, lowest in dry and cold forests; plantings are not in their map, so this is a judgment from it. The national-forest plantings are mostly western conifers on burned land, slow in their first decade and faster after. Our judgment, 3 t CO₂ (1 to 6) averaged over the growth years below.

rows.label: Forests: years a replanted stand keeps taking up carbon at that rate
rows.explainer: Western conifer stands keep adding carbon for many decades before growth slows. Our judgment, 50 years (30 to 80); losses to later fire are in the evidence row.

rows.label: Forests: CO₂ the acres planted in a year take up over their growth, discounted
rows.explainer: Each year's plantings take up carbon for decades: acres in hectares (facts: climate.ha_per_acre) × uptake a year × the growth years, each year's uptake discounted at the shared rate. This is what a year of the won programme adds, counted like the other branches for the years a won reform counts.

rows.label: Share of each win due to advocacy at all (all groups together)
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts: climate.advocacy_share_of_policy_win, 30%, 10% to 60%): the part of a won policy that is the advocates' doing rather than what Congress, agencies, companies and events would have done at the same time. Every win below takes it; Carbon180's part of the advocates' work is each branch's attribution row. The wins are in, so this is not a chance of winning.

rows.label: Years a won reform counts before it would have come anyway
rows.explainer: The site's one answer (docs/normalization.md 2.9).

rows.label: Years a win counts, discounted
Years from a won credit or programme until its tonnes are avoided (the 45Q, farm and forest branches)
rows.explainer: The shared figure for rules, tax credits and programme money (facts: climate.years_until_avoided_regulation, 3 years, 1 to 6); the direct air capture plants and the technology have their own waits below.

rows.label: Discount for the wait until the tonnes are avoided (the 45Q, farm and forest branches)
rows.explainer: The wait discounted at the shared rate; the unit's conversion then discounts the heat deaths from the year the tonne is avoided, so nothing is discounted twice.

rows.label: Discounted years of impact (the 45Q, farm and forest branches)
Direct air capture plants: years from the wins until the tonnes are removed
rows.explainer: The plants' own dates: the laws of 2021-2022, STRATOS starting in 2026-2027, Project Cypress at full capacity about 2030 (DOE, April 2026), the South Texas hub's first phase later. Our judgment, 6 years (4 to 9).

rows.label: Direct air capture plants: discounted years of impact
Technology: share of the IEA pathway's direct air capture that gets built
rows.explainer: The pathway needs about 600 million tonnes a year by 2050 from about 0.01 million in 2023; the plants running in 2025 capture tens of thousands of tonnes, several run below their design (Climeworks' Orca and Mammoth), costs are still several hundred dollars a tonne, and buyers beyond a few technology firms are scarce. This share carries all of that, so the technology branch takes no evidence discount for it. Reference class: the advanced-nuclear pathway in Clean Air Task Force's model, 30% built, for a technology already proven at scale; direct air capture is earlier and dearer. Our judgment, 15% (3% to 50%).

rows.label: Technology: share of that deployment due to the period's US carbon-removal programmes
rows.explainer: The wins of 2020-2025 that speed the technology rather than the first plants alone: the Department of Energy's carbon-removal research programmes (the Energy Act of 2020; about $116.5 million a year, held in the 2026 appropriations), learning by doing on the first megaton plants the hubs and the $180 credit pay for, and the $35 million purchase prize. Anchor: in mid-2024 all 53 direct air capture plants running in the US, Canada and Europe captured about 0.1 million tonnes a year (Third Way 2024, https://www.thirdway.org/memo/status-report-american-competitiveness-in-direct-air-capture.pdf: 'capturing about 0.1 Mt of carbon annually'), so the three US plants' 2.5 million tonnes of design capacity are 25 times all of it. But cost declines come from deployment worldwide and from buyers (Frontier's $925 million advance commitment, Microsoft), and Europe, Canada and Japan support it too. Our judgment, 8% (2% to 20%).

rows.label: Technology: years from the wins until the tonnes are removed
rows.explainer: The shared figure for technologies not yet deployed at scale (facts: climate.years_until_avoided_technology, 15 years, 8 to 25).

rows.label: Technology: discounted years of impact
Technology: the middle of the years the speed-up counts
rows.explainer: The period's middle year plus the wait until the tonnes come plus half the years a won reform counts: about 2040 at the defaults. The pathway's level is read in that year, so the wait and the tonnes describe the same years.

rows.label: Technology: direct air capture on the IEA pathway in the years counted
rows.explainer: The pathway's level in the middle of the years counted, straight-line between its 2030 and 2050 points (about 335 million tonnes a year at the defaults), held at the 2050 level beyond.

rows.label: Direct air capture plants: expected tonnes, before adjustments
Technology: expected tonnes, before adjustments
rows.formula: tech_pathway_tonnes_counted * tech_deployment_share * tech_policy_share * dac_net_removal_share * p_success * tech_discounted_years

rows.label: 45Q at other plants: expected tonnes, before adjustments
Farm conservation money: expected tonnes, before adjustments
Forests: expected tonnes, before adjustments
Expected tonnes a year of the period, before adjustments
rows.explainer: The five branches, each its tonnes a year × the advocacy share × its discounted years (× the built and policy shares for the technology), summed and spread over the period's six years.

rows.label: Direct air capture plants: evidence adjustment (plants running below design once built)
rows.explainer: The tonnes are design capacities, not measured removals, and the first direct air capture plants have run well below design once built (Climeworks' Orca and Mammoth); whether the plants get built at all is the implementation row below, not here. Our judgment, 0.7 (0.4 to 1.0).

rows.label: Technology: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: The built share already prices plants running below design and slow build-out, so only the error of reading a pathway at all is left here. Our judgment, 1 (0.8 to 1).

rows.label: 45Q at other plants: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: The shared figure already cuts the 2022 projection to about a third for pipelines and storage permits built slower than projected (facts: climate.ira_45q_capture_tco2_per_year), so only modelling error is left here. Our judgment, 1 (0.85 to 1).

rows.label: Farm conservation money: evidence adjustment (working farms, practices kept)
rows.explainer: The shared soil-carbon figure already covers the doubt about trials and measurement; what is left is that gains on working farms run below trial plots and are lost when a practice stops after payments end. Our judgment, 0.7 (0.4 to 1).

rows.label: Forests: evidence adjustment (seedlings surviving, stands lost to fire)
rows.explainer: Many planted seedlings die in the first years on dry burned sites, and western stands face rising fire risk over the decades counted. Our judgment, 0.5 (0.25 to 0.8).

rows.label: Evidence adjustment (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.formula: (dac_downstream * dac_evidence_adj + tech_downstream * tech_evidence_adj + q45_downstream * q45_evidence_adj + land_downstream * land_evidence_adj + forest_downstream * forest_evidence_adj) / (dac_downstream + tech_downstream + q45_downstream + land_downstream + forest_downstream)
rows.explainer: The branches' own rows apply; this is their average, weighted by each branch's expected tonnes before adjustments, for reading only.

rows.label: Direct air capture plants: share of the tonnes that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: Without the hub grants and the $180 credit no megaton plant would be built in the US this decade (the voluntary price of a tonne removed by direct air capture is several hundred dollars, and buyers are few). Some of the removal sold to companies replaces removal they would have bought elsewhere (forests, biochar, weathering), which this counts against the plants. What the public money that pays for them costs taxpayers is the branch's own row (dac_public_cost_uov, docs/normalization.md 2.23). Our judgment, 75% (50% to 95%).

rows.label: Direct air capture plants: Carbon180's share of the advocacy resources behind the wins
rows.explainer: Carbon180 says its policy team helped structure the hubs programme in the 2021 law and shaped the hubs' design and their 2025 defence (annual reports 2021, 2022 and 2025). Budgets in 2022 (Form 990s, total expenses): Clean Air Task Force $40.5M, the Bipartisan Policy Center $32.2M, Third Way Institute $18.6M, the Great Plains Institute, which convenes the Carbon Capture Coalition, $7.4M (year to June 2022), Carbon180 $7.1M. Each × the share it spent on carbon capture and removal (judged: 15%, 5%, 10%, 25%, 60%) gives $6.1M, $1.6M, $1.9M, $1.9M and Carbon180's $4.3M, 27% of the groups' resources. The companies' own lobbying (Occidental, Climeworks, Heirloom, the DAC Coalition's members) and ClearPath, judged at one and a half times the groups together, bring it to about 11%; lobbying filings report one amount across all issues, so they can't split this further. Our judgment, 10% (4% to 25%).

rows.label: Direct air capture plants: share of credit used
Direct air capture plants: share of the plants' tonnes delivered
rows.explainer: The hub awards were on DOE's 2025 termination list and kept in April 2026 with only $50 million each obligated (of up to $600M and $500M); STRATOS has slipped by two years; the South Texas hub's first phase is half its design; the 2025 budget law kept the 45Q credit. Our judgment, 45% (15% to 80%) of the design tonnes.

rows.label: Technology: share of the tonnes that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: Removal brought forward may replace other removal or cuts the same buyers and governments would have paid for. Our judgment, 70% (40% to 100%), as in Clean Air Task Force's advanced-nuclear branch.

rows.label: Technology: Carbon180's share of the advocacy resources behind the programmes
rows.explainer: As for the plants (the groups' 2022 budgets on carbon capture and removal, about $15.8M with Carbon180's $4.3M, and the companies at one and a half times that), plus the universities and national laboratories behind the research money, judged at three-quarters of the groups again: about 8%. Carbon180's $4.3M counts in both this and the plants' share, since the same team worked on both. Carbon180 says it secured the first $60 million of carbon-removal appropriations in 2019 and wrote appropriations requests every year since. Our judgment, 8% (3% to 20%).

rows.label: Technology: share of credit used
Technology: share of the programmes delivered
rows.explainer: The hubs programme stands at $1.2 billion kept of $3.5 billion appropriated, the research money held flat, the purchase prize paid in part; the 45Q credit for direct air capture survived the 2025 law. Our judgment, 50% (25% to 85%).

rows.label: 45Q at other plants: share of the tonnes that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: Share of the stored tonnes that are real cuts: a few capture projects sit on plants that would otherwise have closed or cut emissions another way; the tonnes are already only those due to the larger credit. Our judgment, 90% (70% to 100%), as in Clean Air Task Force's model for the same credit.

rows.label: 45Q at other plants: Carbon180's share of the advocacy resources behind the larger credit
rows.explainer: Carbon180 worked on 45Q for direct air capture and says its coalition work helped keep the credit in 2025; it doesn't campaign for capture at fossil plants ('CDR ≠ CCS'). The larger credit for those plants was carried by the Carbon Capture Coalition's more than 100 companies, unions and groups, Clean Air Task Force and the industries that claim it; lobbying filings cover many issues at once and can't be split by provision. Our judgment, 0.3% (0.1% to 1.5%), a tenth of Clean Air Task Force's 3%.

rows.label: 45Q at other plants: share of credit used
45Q at other plants: share of the credit's tonnes delivered (repeal and claw-back risk)
rows.explainer: Slow build-out is already in the shared tonnes; what is left is the credit being cut or clawed back. The 2025 budget law kept 45Q (and gave used carbon the stored rate) while cutting most other clean-energy credits. Our judgment, 95% (80% to 100%).

rows.label: Side effect: extra oil from captured CO₂ used to push oil out of old wells, as a share of the 45Q branch
rows.explainer: Part of the CO₂ stored under 45Q at other plants goes to enhanced oil recovery, which keeps old fields producing, and the 2025 law gave that use the full credit; the extra oil burned offsets part of the stored tonnes. Our judgment, −8% of the branch (−20% to 0), the same per branch as Clean Air Task Force's −1% of a model whose capture branch is an eighth of it.

rows.label: Farm conservation money: share of the tonnes that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: The conservation programmes (EQIP, CSP) were oversubscribed before the law, so the money funded extra contracts, but some paid farmers would have adopted the practices anyway, and some practices replace others already in place. Our judgment, 50% (25% to 80%).

rows.label: Farm conservation money: Carbon180's share of the advocacy resources behind it
rows.explainer: Carbon180's 2022 annual report says its advocacy was 'realized' in the law's conservation investments; its land team took about a sixth of its $7.1M in 2022 ($1.2M, judged). The agriculture title was carried by the National Sustainable Agriculture Coalition, American Farmland Trust, The Nature Conservancy's and Environmental Defense Fund's agriculture programmes, the farm groups and the committees' own staff, together judged at about fifty times Carbon180's land team. Our judgment, 2% (0.5% to 6%).

rows.label: Farm conservation money: share of credit used
Farm conservation money: share of the funded practices delivered with their climate focus
rows.explainer: The 2025 budget law rescinded the Inflation Reduction Act's unobligated conservation money and moved it into the programmes' ordinary funding without its climate targeting; contracts already signed run on, and some practices lapse when payments end. Our judgment, 50% (25% to 80%) of the counted years.

rows.label: Forests: share of the plantings that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: The capped fund paid about a fifth of today's yearly reforestation money, and other Forest Service budgets and partners also plant; some burned land would regrow naturally. Our judgment, 70% (50% to 85%).

rows.label: Forests: Carbon180's share of the advocacy resources behind the reforestation money
rows.explainer: American Forests led the REPLANT Act's coalition of more than 100 groups (the state foresters, the Society of American Foresters, conservation and timber groups); Carbon180's forestry work was a small part of its $3.6M in 2021 (about $0.2M, judged), against a coalition judged at about fifty times that. Our judgment, 2% (0.5% to 6%).

rows.label: Forests: share of credit used
Forests: share of the programme delivered
rows.explainer: The cap's removal is permanent and the fund is paid from tariffs on imported wood, but the Forest Service lost much of its staff in 2025, and planting needs nurseries and crews. Our judgment, 75% (50% to 95%).

rows.label: Counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity
rows.explainer: The shared missing-data step (docs/normalization.md 2.12): no tonne is measured for Carbon180's work. The tonnes are design capacities and projections of whole programmes, and its part in them a judgment. Every branch takes it.

rows.label: Direct air capture plants: all adjustments combined
Technology: all adjustments combined
45Q at other plants: all adjustments combined
Farm conservation money: all adjustments combined
Forests: all adjustments combined
Share of the tonnes that wouldn't have happened anyway (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.formula: (dac_downstream * dac_counterfactual_adj + tech_downstream * tech_counterfactual_adj + q45_downstream * q45_counterfactual_adj + land_downstream * land_counterfactual_adj + forest_downstream * forest_counterfactual_adj) / (dac_downstream + tech_downstream + q45_downstream + land_downstream + forest_downstream)
rows.explainer: The branches' own rows apply; this is their average, weighted by each branch's expected tonnes before adjustments, for reading only.

rows.label: Carbon180's share of the resources behind the wins (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.formula: (dac_downstream * dac_counterfactual_adj * dac_attribution_share_shared + tech_downstream * tech_counterfactual_adj * tech_attribution_share_shared + q45_downstream * q45_counterfactual_adj * q45_attribution_share_shared + land_downstream * land_counterfactual_adj * land_attribution_share_shared + forest_downstream * forest_counterfactual_adj * forest_attribution_share_shared) / (dac_downstream * dac_counterfactual_adj + tech_downstream * tech_counterfactual_adj + q45_downstream * q45_counterfactual_adj + land_downstream * land_counterfactual_adj + forest_downstream * forest_counterfactual_adj)
rows.explainer: The branches' own rows apply; this is their average, weighted by each branch's tonnes after the counterfactual, for reading only.

rows.label: Share of credit used (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.explainer: The outcome-weighted average of the branches' credit shares, for reading only; each branch applies its own.

rows.label: Share of the wins' tonnes delivered (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.formula: (dac_downstream * dac_counterfactual_adj * dac_attribution_share * dac_implementation_adj + tech_downstream * tech_counterfactual_adj * tech_attribution_share * tech_implementation_adj + q45_downstream * q45_counterfactual_adj * q45_attribution_share * q45_implementation_adj + land_downstream * land_counterfactual_adj * land_attribution_share * land_implementation_adj + forest_downstream * forest_counterfactual_adj * forest_attribution_share * forest_implementation_adj) / (dac_downstream * dac_counterfactual_adj * dac_attribution_share + tech_downstream * tech_counterfactual_adj * tech_attribution_share + q45_downstream * q45_counterfactual_adj * q45_attribution_share + land_downstream * land_counterfactual_adj * land_attribution_share + forest_downstream * forest_counterfactual_adj * forest_attribution_share)
rows.explainer: The branches' own rows apply; this is their average, weighted by each branch's tonnes after the counterfactual and credit, for reading only.

rows.label: Other work of the period not modelled, as a share of the modelled value
rows.explainer: What the five branches leave out: ocean carbon-removal research ($10.5M at NOAA in 2025, the first bicameral bill in 2026: an addition to the research in the technology branch), the 2025 forestry appropriations it worked on ($37M for urban and community forestry, $32M for the forest inventory, $2M for agroforestry: funding held at earlier levels), the CORE standards framework, the community regranting ($0.9M in 2025) and the newsletters and briefings. Their spending is in the cost, so leaving them out would count them as worth nothing. Our judgment, 5% of the modelled value (2% to 15%).

rows.label: Side effect: emission cuts put off because removal is promised, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Promises of future removal can let companies and governments delay cuts ('mitigation deterrence'; McLaren et al. 2019); Carbon180's standards and accountability work pushes the other way, and the tonnes counted here are physical removals. Our judgment, −5% (−20% to 0).

rows.label: All adjustments combined (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.formula: (dac_downstream * dac_total_adj + tech_downstream * tech_total_adj + q45_downstream * q45_total_adj + land_downstream * land_total_adj + forest_downstream * forest_total_adj) / (dac_downstream + tech_downstream + q45_downstream + land_downstream + forest_downstream)
rows.explainer: The branches' own combined adjustments apply; this is their average, weighted by each branch's expected tonnes before adjustments, for reading only. The wins are tax credits, grants and research and conservation money, not rules, so no compliance cost is counted (docs/normalization.md 2.21: public money is not a compliance cost). What the public money costs taxpayers is netted in each branch's public-cost row (docs/normalization.md 2.23).

rows.label: Value lost per dollar of US public money, units of value
rows.explainer: What a dollar of federal money costs those who pay for it (docs/normalization.md 2.23): the shared cost of raising it (facts: public_funds.mcpf) over federal taxpayers' consumption on the survey scale (the shared payer multiple × US consumption per person, 2.14), on the log scale.

rows.label: 45Q at other plants: public money a year for the stored tonnes
rows.explainer: The credit the Treasury pays for each tonne stored (facts: climate.q45_credit_usd_per_tco2, $85) × the branch's tonnes.

rows.label: 45Q at other plants: what that money costs its payers, units of value (negative)
rows.explainer: Public money that buys tonnes is netted against its payers' loss (docs/normalization.md 2.23), over the branch's years, wait, advocacy share and every adjustment of its tonnes, since the credit is paid per tonne stored.

rows.label: Direct air capture plants: public money a year (credit and hub grants)
rows.explainer: The $180 credit for each tonne captured and stored (facts: climate.q45_credit_usd_per_tco2_dac) × the plants' gross tonnes; the hub grants are in the next row.

rows.label: Direct air capture plants: what that money costs its payers, units of value (negative)
rows.formula: -(dac_public_usd_per_year * dac_total_adj + dac_hub_grants_usd / @climate.q45_credit_years * dac_total_adj / dac_evidence_adj) * public_payer_uov_per_dollar * p_success * dac_discounted_years
rows.explainer: The credit, paid per tonne, takes every adjustment of the plants' tonnes; the hub grants, a fixed sum spread over the credit's 12 years (facts: climate.q45_credit_years), all but the evidence step, which is about the tonnes (docs/normalization.md 2.23).

rows.label: Technology: what the public money costs its payers, units of value (negative)
rows.formula: -(tech_pathway_tonnes_counted * tech_deployment_share * tech_policy_share * tech_public_usd_per_tco2 * tech_total_adj + tech_research_usd_per_year * tech_total_adj / tech_evidence_adj) * public_payer_uov_per_dollar * p_success * tech_discounted_years
rows.explainer: The removals the faster build brings, bought with public money (row tech_public_usd_per_tco2, per tonne captured), with every adjustment of the branch's tonnes; and the research money, a fixed sum, without the evidence step (docs/normalization.md 2.23). Rich-country payers, at the US figure.

source.title: USDA NRCS (December 2024), Biden-Harris Administration Delivers Record Investments in Private Lands Conservation
source.quote: obligated 97.6% of all available fiscal year 2024 Inflation Reduction Act conservation program financial assistance funds, or more than $1.6 billion

rows.explainer: The law's conservation money obligated in fiscal 2024 for the climate-focused contracts counted above (11 million acres).

rows.label: Farm conservation money: what it costs its payers, units of value (negative)
rows.explainer: A fixed sum a year, with the branch's years, wait, advocacy share, counterfactual, credit, delivered share and missing-data step, not its evidence step, which is about the tonnes per acre (docs/normalization.md 2.23). The practices' other gains (water, soil) are not counted, like every unmodelled benefit, in unmodelled_benefits_adj.

rows.explainer: Every branch's public money netted against its tonnes (docs/normalization.md 2.23), the input of the bridge into tonnes.

rows.label: Share of these tonnes from burning less fossil fuel near people
rows.explainer: None: direct air capture removes CO₂ from the air, capture at a running plant stores its CO₂ while the plant keeps burning, and soil and forest carbon are land, so no fuel smoke is avoided.
